blocks.content: Every process a computer runs is born, lives for a while, and eventually dies. In between, it does not just run continuously from start to finish. It spends its life moving through a small number of well defined states, sometimes executing on the processor, sometimes patiently waiting its turn, and sometimes blocked and unable to proceed at all until something else happens. Understanding this journey, and exactly what triggers each step of it, is one of the most fundamental ideas in operating systems.

This chapter walks through the process lifecycle from the moment a process is created to the moment it is torn down. You will see the standard set of states every operating system textbook describes, the precise events that move a process from one state to the next, a full worked example that traces a familiar application through its entire life, why this bookkeeping matters so much to the operating system, a common real world elaboration on the basic model, and the misconceptions that trip up almost everyone the first time they meet this topic.

1. Why a Process Needs States at All
blocks.text: 1. Why a Process Needs States at All

blocks.content: A process is a program in execution, and at any given moment a real computer is juggling far more processes than it has processors to run them on. A laptop with four processor cores might comfortably have two hundred processes alive at once. Clearly almost all of them cannot be running at the same instant, so the operating system needs some way to describe what each one is doing right now, whether it is actually executing, merely waiting for a turn, or stuck until some external event occurs.

That description is the process state. Rather than tracking a mess of ad hoc conditions for every process, operating systems settle on a small, fixed set of states that every process passes through, and a clear set of rules for exactly when a process is allowed to move from one state to another. This turns an enormous scheduling problem into something the kernel can manage with simple, predictable bookkeeping.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: The process lifecycle is the sequence of states a process passes through between the moment it is created and the moment it finishes, and the precise events that move it from one state to the next.
2. The Five Standard States
Most operating systems describe a process using five core states. Each one answers a very specific question about what the process is doing right now.

{"headers":["State","What it means"],"rows":[["New","The process is being created. The operating system is setting up its process control block and preparing to admit it into the system."],["Ready","The process is loaded into memory and is eligible to run, but it is waiting for the scheduler to give it a turn on the processor."],["Running","The process is currently executing its instructions on a processor core. Only one process can be running per core at any instant."],["Waiting or Blocked","The process cannot make progress right now because it is waiting for something external, such as an I/O operation to finish or a resource to become free."],["Terminated","The process has finished executing, either by completing normally or by being stopped, and the operating system is cleaning up its resources."]]}
New: the process is being born
blocks.text: New: the process is being born

blocks.content: When a program is launched, the operating system does not instantly turn it into a running process. First it does the work of creation: it allocates a process control block to track the process, sets up an address space for it, and loads the program code and initial data into memory. During this setup the process sits in the New state. It exists as far as the operating system's bookkeeping is concerned, but it has not yet been accepted as a full participant competing for the processor.
Ready: waiting for a turn

Once creation finishes, the operating system admits the process, and it moves into the Ready state. A process in Ready is completely capable of running immediately. It has memory, it has everything it needs, and the only thing standing between it and execution is that the processor is busy with someone else. All ready processes sit together in a structure often called the ready queue, and the scheduler picks among them.
Running: executing on the processor

A process in the Running state is the one actually being executed by a processor core right now. Its instructions are being fetched and carried out. On a single core machine, exactly one process can be running at any instant. On a machine with several cores, several processes can be running simultaneously, one per core, but never more than one per core at a time.
Waiting or Blocked: stuck until something happens
blocks.text: Waiting or Blocked: stuck until something happens

blocks.content: A process enters the Waiting state, also commonly called Blocked, when it cannot proceed no matter how much processor time it is given. The classic trigger is requesting an I/O operation, such as reading from disk or waiting for network data, but a process can also block on a lock, a semaphore, or any event it depends on that has not happened yet. Giving a waiting process the processor would accomplish nothing, since it has no useful work to do until that external event arrives.
Terminated: the process is done

A process reaches Terminated when it finishes its work, whether by returning normally from its main routine, calling an explicit exit, or being killed by the operating system or another process. In this state the operating system reclaims the memory, closes any open files and handles, and eventually removes the process control block once any parent process has collected its exit status.
3. Transitions Between States

What makes this model powerful is not just the five states themselves, but the strict rules about which transitions are allowed and exactly what triggers each one. A process can never jump arbitrarily between states. Every move is caused by a specific, identifiable event.

["New to Ready happens after admission by the operating system, once creation is complete and the process is accepted to compete for the processor.","Ready to Running happens when the scheduler dispatches the process, choosing it from the ready queue and handing it a processor core.","Running to Ready happens on a timer interrupt or preemption, when the process's time slice runs out or a higher priority process needs to run.","Running to Waiting happens when the process requests I/O or blocks on a resource that is not immediately available.","Waiting to Ready happens when the awaited event completes, such as the disk finishing a read or a lock becoming free.","Running to Terminated happens on exit, when the process finishes its work or is stopped."]
items: New to Ready happens after admission by the operating system, once creation is complete and the process is accepted to compete for the processor.
Ready to Running happens when the scheduler dispatches the process, choosing it from the ready queue and handing it a processor core.
Running to Ready happens on a timer interrupt or preemption, when the process's time slice runs out or a higher priority process needs to run.
Running to Waiting happens when the process requests I/O or blocks on a resource that is not immediately available.
Waiting to Ready happens when the awaited event completes, such as the disk finishing a read or a lock becoming free.
Running to Terminated happens on exit, when the process finishes its work or is stopped.

blocks.title: Notice what is missing
blocks.content: There is no direct arrow from Waiting straight to Running, and no arrow from New straight to Running. A process that has just been unblocked, or one that has just been created, must always pass back through Ready and wait to be dispatched by the scheduler. Being eligible to run is not the same thing as actually running.
4. A Worked Example: The Life of a Text Editor
blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example: The Life of a Text Editor

blocks.content: Abstract state names are easier to remember with a concrete story attached to them. Follow a simple text editor process from launch to close, and watch exactly which state it occupies at each moment.

["You double click the text editor icon. The operating system begins creating the process: allocating a process control block, setting up its address space, and loading the program into memory. The process is in the New state.","Creation finishes and the operating system admits the process into the system. It moves to Ready, sitting in the ready queue alongside whatever else is currently waiting for the processor.","The scheduler dispatches the process, giving it a processor core. It moves to Running, and the editor's window appears and becomes responsive.","You choose to open a large file. The editor issues a read request to the disk. Since disk I/O takes far longer than a processor instruction, the process moves to Waiting, and the operating system gives the processor to some other ready process in the meantime.","The disk finishes reading the file's contents into a buffer. The awaited event has completed, so the process moves back to Ready, eligible to run again but not yet actually running.","The scheduler eventually dispatches it again. It returns to Running, parses the file contents, and displays the text so you can start editing.","You finish your edits and close the window. The editor process finishes its cleanup and exits. It moves to Terminated, and the operating system reclaims its memory and closes its open file handles."]
items: You double click the text editor icon. The operating system begins creating the process: allocating a process control block, setting up its address space, and loading the program into memory. The process is in the New state.
Creation finishes and the operating system admits the process into the system. It moves to Ready, sitting in the ready queue alongside whatever else is currently waiting for the processor.
The scheduler dispatches the process, giving it a processor core. It moves to Running, and the editor's window appears and becomes responsive.

You choose to open a large file. The editor issues a read request to the disk. Since disk I/O takes far longer than a processor instruction, the process moves to Waiting, and the operating system gives the processor to some other ready process in the meantime.
The disk finishes reading the file's contents into a buffer. The awaited event has completed, so the process moves back to Ready, eligible to run again but not yet actually running.
The scheduler eventually dispatches it again. It returns to Running, parses the file contents, and displays the text so you can start editing.
You finish your edits and close the window. The editor process finishes its cleanup and exits. It moves to Terminated, and the operating system reclaims its memory and closes its open file handles.

blocks.content: A process rarely runs from start to finish in one unbroken stretch. It is dispatched, runs for a while, blocks on something, gets unblocked, waits again for a turn, and repeats this cycle many times before it finally terminates.
5. Why the Operating System Tracks This So Precisely
blocks.text: 5. Why the Operating System Tracks This So Precisely

blocks.content: It might seem like unnecessary bookkeeping to track exactly which state every process occupies, but this precision is what makes the scheduler correct at all. The operating system relies on process state for several critical decisions, and getting any of them wrong would break the whole system.

["To know which processes are eligible for the processor right now, the scheduler only ever considers processes in the Ready state. It never even looks at processes that are New, Waiting, or Terminated when deciding who to dispatch next.","To know which processes are stuck waiting, so the operating system can hold off on giving them the processor and instead wake them the instant their awaited event completes.","To avoid ever running a process that is not actually ready, which would waste processor cycles on a process that has nothing useful to do and cannot make progress."]
items: To know which processes are eligible for the processor right now, the scheduler only ever considers processes in the Ready state. It never even looks at processes that are New, Waiting, or Terminated when deciding who to dispatch next.
To know which processes are stuck waiting, so the operating system can hold off on giving them the processor and instead wake them the instant their awaited event completes.
To avoid ever running a process that is not actually ready, which would waste processor cycles on a process that has nothing useful to do and cannot make progress.

blocks.content: Every one of these decisions depends on the state being accurate at all times. If the operating system ever dispatched a process that was actually still Waiting on a disk read, that process would simply sit on the processor doing nothing useful, wasting a scarce resource that some genuinely ready process could have used instead.
6. A Real World Elaboration: The Suspended State
blocks.text: 6. A Real World Elaboration: The Suspended State

blocks.content: The five state model captures the essential picture, but some operating systems extend it to handle a practical problem: what happens when there simply is not enough main memory for every process that wants to exist. Under heavy memory pressure, an operating system can move a process out of main memory entirely and onto disk, a technique often called swapping.

A process that has been swapped out this way is described as Suspended, sometimes further split into Suspended Ready and Suspended Waiting depending on what state it was in before it got swapped out. A suspended process cannot run at all, since its memory image is not even present in main memory anymore, and it must first be swapped back in before it can return to the ordinary Ready or Waiting states.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.content: The Suspended state is a pragmatic addition rather than a theoretical requirement. It exists because real machines have finite memory and sometimes need to temporarily set aside a lower priority process to make room for more urgent work, without losing that process's progress entirely.
7. Common Misconceptions
Two mistakes come up constantly when people first learn this material, and both are worth calling out explicitly.
Confusing Waiting with Ready

These two states sound similar but describe completely different situations. Ready means the process could run right now if it were simply given the processor; nothing external is stopping it, it just has not been picked yet. Waiting means the process cannot run even if it were given the processor, because it is blocked on something external, such as an I/O operation that has not finished. Handing the processor to a waiting process would not help it make any progress at all.
Assuming a process only runs once, start to finish
blocks.text: Assuming a process only runs once, start to finish

blocks.content: A process almost never occupies the Running state continuously from creation to termination. It typically cycles through Running and Ready many times as the scheduler shares the processor fairly, and often visits Waiting multiple times whenever it needs I/O or another external resource. The lifecycle is a loop that can repeat many times, not a single straight line.
8. The Interview Angle

A very common interview question is simply to draw the process state diagram from memory and explain what triggers each transition. Interviewers are less interested in whether you can recite the state names and far more interested in whether you can explain, without hesitation, exactly what causes each arrow: admission causing New to Ready, dispatch causing Ready to Running, preemption or a timer interrupt causing Running back to Ready, an I/O or resource request causing Running to Waiting, and the completion of that awaited event causing Waiting back to Ready.

A strong answer also volunteers the detail that there is no direct path from Waiting to Running, and explains why: a process that just got unblocked still has to wait its turn like everyone else in the ready queue. Mentioning the Suspended state as a practical extension used under memory pressure is a good way to show depth beyond the textbook basics, provided you can also explain clearly why it exists.

blocks.title: Quick recap to keep ready
blocks.content: Five states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting or Blocked, Terminated. Six transitions: admitted, dispatched, preempted, blocks on I/O or a resource, event completes, exits. Ready means eligible to run; Waiting means blocked on something external.
